newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Two Russian cosmonauts land safely on earth.
newsitem.headline: Two Russian cosmonauts land safely on earth.

text.p: Two Russian cosmonauts who spent six months on the Mir space station landed safely in the steppes of Kazakhstan on Thursday after one of the toughest missions in the history of manned space flight.

This correspondent saw Commander Vasily Tsibliyev and flight engineer Alexander Lazutkin after their Soyuz capsule, dangling beneath a huge white and yellow parachute, landed near the town of Dzhezkazgan shortly before 4:20 p.m. Moscow time (1220 GMT), slightly behind schedule.
The two, looking tired but well, smiled broadly as they emerged from their craft. Tsibliyev, who seemed to be the more animated of the two, said he felt "happy to be back on earth".
The cosmonauts have endured a series of major woes since they arrived aboard Mir in February. The most serious was a June 25 collision between the station and its supply ship.
Mir has run on partial power since then. They also had to contend with a fire and a series of problems with their life support systems during their mission.
Helicopters bearing rescue teams clattered to the remote desert site where Soyuz landed and doctors carried out extensive medical checks on the cosmonauts.
They said their heart and pulse rates were satisfactory. There had been some concern about the health of Tsibliyev, 43, who developed a stress-related cardiac problem while on Mir.
Live television pictures at Mission Control outside Moscow had shown Soyuz with Tsibliyev, and Lazutkin, 39, on board departing from Mir at 12:56 p.m. Moscow time (0856 GMT).
There appeared to be a three-minute delay in the operation compared to the original schedule but a Mission Control operator said the undocking went well.
"Everything is all right with you," the operator told the crew. "Thank God," replied Tsibliyev.
Tsibliyev and Lazutkin have left British-born Michael Foale and their two Russian replacements, Commander Anatoly Solovyov and engineer Pavel Vinogradov, aboard Mir.
"I hope that everything bad that we've had will leave with us," Tsibliyev said in a live broadcast from Mir.
"We are leaving. See you on earth."
A Mission Control operator told Tsibliyev and Lazutkin: "Thank you for the job you've done. Happy landing."
The cosmonauts wore lightweight spacesuits during their return, each weighing 10 kg with independent air supply systems.
The light spacesuits were introduced in 1973 after three Soviet cosmonauts -- Georgy Dobrovolsky, Vladislav Volkov and Viktor Patsayev -- died during descent in 1971 in a capsule which lost air.

Despite the warm welcome for the two men on Thursday, Tsibliyev and Lazutkin face an uncertain reception on earth. President Boris Yeltsin said last week human error may have been to blame for the June 25 crash, which threatened Mir's future.
But Yeltsin's space and aviation aide, Marshal Yevgeny Shaposhnikov told Interfax news agency on Thursday no hasty conclusions should be drawn until a proper investigation into the accident.

After their medical checks, the cosmonauts were due to be taken by helicopter to Dzhezkazgan. From there they were expected to travel by plane to Chkalovsky military airbase near Moscow, then a bus will take them to the Star City training centre.
"They may go home after seven or 10 days, but they will be able to see their families during this period," said Pyotr Klimuk, head of the Cosmonauts' Training Centre.
